subject: physics
title: Atomic, Nuclear & Particle Physics Adventure 2: Radioactive decay and nuclear stability
welcome_lead: Today you'll watch atoms decay via α, β, γ — with half-life math.
meta_desc: Physics — α, β, γ decay, decay equation N = N₀e^(-λt), half-life, binding energy.
final_note: You learned α (He-4), β (e⁻ from neutron), γ (photon) emissions; N = N₀e^(-λt); t½ = ln2/λ; binding energy holds nucleus.

walkthroughs.body_html:
- α decay: heavy nucleus emits ⁴He²⁺. A−4, Z−2. ²³⁸U → ²³⁴Th + α.
- β⁻ decay: neutron-rich; n → p + e⁻ + ν̄. A unchanged, Z+1. ¹⁴C → ¹⁴N + β⁻.
- γ decay: nucleus drops to lower state, emits high-energy photon. A, Z unchanged.

Number decays at rate proportional to N:

N(t) = N₀ · e^(-λt)

where λ = decay constant.

Half-life: t½ = ln2/λ ≈ 0.693/λ.

After n half-lives, fraction remaining = (1/2)ⁿ.

Nuclear mass < sum of nucleon masses — difference = mass defect Δm.

Binding energy ΔE = Δm · c².

Binding energy per nucleon peaks at ⁵⁶Fe (~8.8 MeV).

Fission (split heavy) and fusion (combine light) both release energy by reaching more stable nuclei.

¹⁴C dating (t½ = 5730 y) — used to date organic remains up to ~50,000 y.

Is the internal energy of a system the same as the heat it contains?
options: It reflects them back the way they came.
No — a system doesn't 'contain heat'; internal energy is the total kinetic and potential energy of its particles, changed by heating or doing work.
Yes — internal energy is just the stored heat in the object.
No — internal energy refers only to the chemical potential energy.

mcqs.q: What does a concave lens do to parallel rays of light?
options: Because the plates are uniform in shape.
It diverges them — they spread out as if from a virtual focal point behind the lens.
It reflects them back the way they came.
It converges them to a focal point in front of the lens.

mcqs.q: Why is the electric field between parallel charged plates considered uniform?
options: It reflects them back the way they came.
Because the plates are uniform in shape.
Field strength is constant in magnitude and direction throughout the region (away from edges), unlike the inverse-square field of a point charge.
The field still decreases with the inverse square of distance — uniform just means it's smooth.
